newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania sees rising crime, needs new laws-police.
newsitem.headline: Romania sees rising crime, needs new laws-police.

text.p: Romania's top policeman called on Tuesday for a complete overhaul of the legal system to tackle increasing and more diverse crime afflicting the country in the seven years since it shed communism.

"Romania's penal system remains mired in the requirements of the 1960s, when the totalitarian regime was entrenched," General Pavel Abraham told a news conference marking National Police Day. "We have to make a clear 180 degree turn to bring in new procedures and regulations."

His remarks followed accusations by Romanian media that reformist President Emil Constantinescu's much-publicised crusade against organised crime and corruption had yielded meagre results since he took office last November.

Constantinescu and the centrist coalition government created a "National Committee to Fight Organised Crime" after intelligence service reports showed that the shadow economy accounted for almost 40 percent of the gross domestic product.
The president and ministers issue frequent reports quoting sums of money they say have been reclaimed.
But Abraham, head of Romania's national police force, said current laws had failed to produce a guilty verdict in a single major case of corruption.

"The law is applied in whatever way is deemed proper by officials. When it suits the authorities, they apply the system as it is. When it doesn't, they say it is inappropriate to the new democracy," he said.
"Thousands of cases have been launched but only scant hundreds are brought to a conclusion. This must change."
Romania, like all ex-communist countries in Central and Eastern Europe, has experienced soaring organised and common crime in the seven years since the end of tough communist rule.
After Romania opened its borders in 1989 and moved towards a market economy, it has been prey to crimes from tax evasion to illegal trade in weapons, drugs and radioactive material.

Despite shortages of staff, experience and equipment, police last year seized 318 kg (700 pounds) of radioactive material, 15 kg (33 pounds) of nuclear fuel, 2.5 tonnes of explosives and 5.8 tonnes of various drugs.
Abraham said that since 1989, the number of crimes committed, from tax evasion to crimes of violence, had risen annually by 30 percent.

In the first half of 1997, police had solved 194,000 cases, 14 percent more than the same period last year. A quarter were economic crimes and half were committed by minors. Police put losses from crime this year at the equivalent of $108 million.
